How does the fcc censoring cuss words on tv, not go against the freedom of speech amendment?

The US government gave the FCC the power to administer the airwaves as a public trust. Without this power, one bad actor could deliberately (or even inadvertently) create a device that would spew enough radio noise to completely prevent all am/fm radio, TV, cell phone, WiFi, GPS, etc devices from working. If somebody tried to make a radio station on the same frequencies that GPS uses, there is no way the little hand held receivers would be able to pick up the faint signals from the satellites. So that is generally a good thing to regulate.

In the early days of radio and TV, they figured, "Well we are supposed to regulate this for the public good. So we should regulate the content of what is being transmitted, not just the frequencies being used." Swearing (as well as nudity, and so on) was thought to not be in the public interest, so the licensing needed to broadcast TV or radio was set up to prohibit it.

There used to be a lot more regulations on content. Many of those have been phased out.

Edit: As another user pointed out, the FCC doesn't regulate the content of cable broadcasts. It doesn't use the airwaves and thus is not subject to the same rules. Also, by the time satellite transmission was being used for consumer use (DirecTV, Sirius, XM, etc.) there was less of an impetus for regulating content.

At one point licensing was mostly a perfunctory thing done to keep the airwaves clear of competition contention, but after a while the FCC started holding those licenses over companies' heads: either play by its rules or don't get yours renewed. Before then broadcasters still had to deal with standing regulations on decency(most of which were later struck down), but they tended to have more leeway than with with the FCC(the "Wasteland Speech" being a big turning point - nobody wants to piss off the guy who already thinks your medium's full of crap).

Long story short the FCC can't bar viewpoints but the Supreme Court says they can restrict "offensive material" if children are likely to see it. The FCC actually has a whole page devoted to this topic on their website.

Okay, so this gets complicated, but the Administrative Procedure Act essentially allows Congress to delegate the actual implementation of laws to 3rd party organizations, as long as the rules implemented aren't Arbitrary or Capricious- legally defined terms.

From there, two SCOTUS decisions define the FCC's power to censor. First is FCC vs. Pacifica Foundation which held that censoring deliberately obscene material is not a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act.

The second is FCC vs. Fox Television which held that censoring occasional indecent material was also not a violation of the APA.

There has also been a great deal of criticism of the APA, saying that delegating power to non-elected bodies is unconstitutional. This has been reinforced by criticisms of IRS rules and more recently 3rd party legal interpretations of the ACA.
